title: He Could Only Say One Syllable for 21 Years, Yet Understood Every Word
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Paul Broca (1861) & Nina Dronkers (2007): Patient 'Tan', the Preserved Paris Brain & the Birth of Cortical Localization, grounded in Paul Broca (2011) ([English translation of Paul Broca's April 18, 1861 Bulletins de la Société Anatomique de Paris report on Louis Victor Leborgne ('Tan')]). Empirical findings show that in early April 1861 in Paris, fierce scientific debate raged at the Société d'Anthropologie: holistic orthodoxy (Pierre Flourens) insisted the cerebral cortex was an undifferentiated whole after phrenology's collapse, while Ernest Auburtin vowed he would renounce localization forever if a patient lost speech WITHOUT frontal-lobe damage.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how Wernicke's area, Broca's area, white matter coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that just days later (April 12, 1861), 51-year-old Louis Victor Leborgne arrived on surgeon Paul Broca's ward at Bicêtre Hospital — nicknamed 'Monsieur Tan' across the hospital because for 21 years his sole spoken output to almost every question was 'Tan, tan!' (plus one frustrated French oath when angry!).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Paul Broca (2011). Remarks on the Seat of Spoken Language, Followed by a Case of Aphasia (1861). Neuropsychology Review. [English translation of Paul Broca's April 18, 1861 Bulletins de la Société Anatomique de Paris report on Louis Victor Leborgne ('Tan')]. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11065-011-9174-x
- Evelina Fedorenko, Idan A. Blank (2020). Broca’s Area Is Not a Natural Kind. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2020.01.001
- Francis Schiller (1983). Paul Broca and the history of aphasia. Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1212/wnl.33.5.667
